name: Harborland
label: Harborland
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5638327221: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kobe Harborland'.
notes: Waterfront shopping and entertainment area with a Ferris wheel.

text.description:
Harborland is a shopping district in Chuo-ku, Kobe, and it is where Kobe Port Tower stands. The area has a tidy, modern feel, so it suits easy phone photography: wide open spaces, big buildings and plenty of lines to build a picture around.

There is some history behind the view. The land was once a freight yard belonging to the Japanese National Railways. The yard was removed in 1982 and the shopping district opened in 1992.

The phone icon on the map is not in the middle of Harborland. It is about 449 m to the north-east of the district's centre point, so you see Harborland from a little way off, with more of its surroundings in the frame. Treat it as a place to take in the whole scene before you walk closer for details.

From the phone icon on the map, start with the default lens (1x) for a straightforward view of the district. Then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the sky and the surroundings. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the Port Tower and other distant shapes without walking any closer. Turn on the gridlines so the horizon and the tall buildings stay straight. Once you have the wide view, walk into the district for close-ups of the shopfronts and people strolling.
text.geographic_location: Harborland is in Chuo-ku, Kobe, on the site of a former railway freight yard. Kobe Port Tower is in the district.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so use a map app to navigate to the stand-here coordinates (34.680347, 135.18468). Head south-west and the district opens up ahead of you. The phone icon on the map is about 450 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall view. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for more sky and surroundings, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant details such as the Port Tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 450 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line so buildings and sky stay balanced. Keep the phone level so tall structures do not lean. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then zoom in for a tighter picture of the main shapes. Afterwards, walk into the district for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the main building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. In the evening, switch to night mode and hold the phone steady for a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or early evening usually gives softer, more even light than midday. After dark, the district is worth a try with night mode if the lights are on.

text.access_note: Harborland is a shopping district, so it is generally easy to walk around, but individual attractions may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking south-west from the stand-here point, the sun is more likely to be in front of the camera in the afternoon, so morning or early evening light is usually easier.

name: Nankin-machi
label: Nankinmachi Chinatown
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/283443790: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nankinmachi' (289 m across).
notes: Colourful Chinatown with its gates and street food.

text.description:
Nankin-machi is Kobe's Chinatown, a compact network of streets packed with Chinese restaurants, food stalls and shops. It began in 1868, when Kobe's port opened to foreign traders and Chinese settlers made their home at the western edge of the foreign district. The area was destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt by the Chinese community that stayed on. It was badly hit again by the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake, then rebuilt once more.

It photographs well because so much happens within a few steps. Three decorative archways mark the way in: Chang'an Gate to the east (put up in 1985), Xi'an Gate to the west and Nanlou Gate to the south. A pair of lions guards the northern entrance. At the crossing of the two main streets stands a pavilion with stone carvings of the 12 zodiac animals, a popular spot for photos. Between the gates you can shoot food on display, such as dumplings, buns and pastries, along with shopfronts and busy street scenes.

Take a few photos here, then walk to a gate or the pavilion for a different view. Start with the wide street scene, then move in close on the food and the carvings.
text.geographic_location: Nankin-machi is in central Kobe, just south of Motomachi station and next to the Daimaru department store. It is the city's Chinatown.
text.directions_text: Start from the Motomachi area, south of Motomachi station beside the Daimaru department store, and walk south into the Chinatown streets. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the gates and the packed streets, and the default lens (1x) for everyday scenes. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the zodiac carvings, lions and food on display.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Turn slowly and look down each street before you choose a shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate or shopfront straight to your lines. Frame a gate with a little street life in front of it to give a sense of scale. Then go in close and fill the frame with one dish, one carving or one lion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the food or carving to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright shopfronts wash out the picture. Use portrait mode for close-ups of food. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone still against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day for emptier streets and easier wide shots. Late afternoon into evening suits atmospheric shots with the shops lit up.

text.access_note: The streets are public and open to walk through, but individual shops, stalls and any events have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The streets are narrow enough that the ultra-wide lens helps with gates and street scenes.
Streets are usually quieter earlier in the day and busier around lunchtime and at weekends.
The area is lit up in the evening, so night mode can work.

name: Kobe Port Tower
label: Kobe Port Tower
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/99457921: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kobe Port Tower' (37 m across).
notes: Red lattice tower on the Kobe waterfront.

text.description: Kobe Port Tower is a slim red landmark that rises 108 m above the port. It was designed by Nikken Sekkei and completed in 1963. Its shape is meant to recall a tsuzumi, a Japanese hand drum, and it was the first tower built using a pipe lattice. The structure is wrapped by 32 red steel staves, said to symbolise a welcome for vessels returning to shore. That curved, open framework makes a clean silhouette, and the red stands out well against sky or water. The tower also has an LED lighting scheme, installed in 2010, with 40 lighting effects, so it can look quite different after dark. It reopened on 26 April 2024 after a long renovation and seismic work. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north-east of the subject. That distance suits a single, tidy shot with the tower as the clear subject, and it lets you include some foreground for a sense of place. Keep the phone upright to fit the full height, and use the gridlines to keep the tower's vertical lines straight. If you want a tighter picture, step in closer or use the telephoto lens rather than cropping later.
text.geographic_location: Kobe Port Tower is in Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo Prefecture, in the port area of the city. It is a landmark of Kobe.
text.directions_text: Walk from there towards the tower, keeping it to your south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole tower with some surroundings. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, cleaner shot of the tower's shape, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close and want the full height.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The tower is to the south-west of you, so face that way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Line the tower up with a vertical grid line and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean. Leave a little sky above the tip, and include something in the foreground to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the red stays rich and the sky does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon through dusk is a good choice: the light is softer, and you can stay on for the tower's lighting as the sky darkens.

text.access_note: The tower's observation floors are a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements; the stand-here point is for photographing the tower from outside.

name: Meriken Park
label: Meriken Park
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

notes: Waterfront park with the Kobe sign and harbour views.

text.description: Meriken Park is a waterfront park in the port city of Kobe, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to take relaxed, open-air photos. The wide, open ground gives you plenty of sky and water in the frame. The park holds the Kobe Port Tower and the Kobe Maritime Museum, along with a memorial to the victims of the Great Hanshin earthquake. The Hotel Okura Kobe and the Kobe Meriken Park Oriental Hotel are also in the park. The name comes from the word 'American', which was commonly rendered as 'Meriken' in the Meiji era, a nice detail if you want to add a caption to your photo. For a phone, the park works best when you pick one clear subject, such as the tower, the museum or the memorial, and use the open space around it to give the picture room. Take a few wide shots to show the harbour setting, then step closer for a tighter picture with one landmark and a strip of water behind it. The memorial is a place of remembrance, so keep your photos respectful and avoid posing in front of it. Walk a little way along the waterfront and the view changes, so it is worth taking pictures at several points rather than staying in one spot.
text.geographic_location: On Kobe's harbour front in the port area, beside the water and close to the Kobe Port Tower and the Kobe Maritime Museum.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach Meriken Park or the Kobe Port Tower. From it, the middle of the park is about 184 m to the south, which is about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the open waterfront and the buildings together. Use the default lens (1x) for most pictures, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon along the top or bottom line so the sky or water has room to breathe. Include some foreground, such as a railing, a path or the water's edge, to give the picture depth. For a tower or building, keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a panorama along the waterfront if you want the whole width of the park, moving the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually gives softer light and lets you add night mode for the lit-up harbour, but any clear day works well.

text.access_note: The park is a waterfront public space, but individual buildings, the museum and the tower may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ikuta Shrine
label: Ikuta Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '楼門' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '楼門' (way/315897887): middle (17 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/677780046: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ikuta Shrine' (255 m across).
notes: Ancient shrine in the heart of Sannomiya.

text.description:
Ikuta Shrine is a Shinto shrine in Kobe's Chūō Ward, and it may be one of the oldest shrines in Japan. According to the Nihon Shoki, Empress Jingū founded it at the start of the 3rd century AD to honour the kami Wakahirume. It is one of three shrines set up at that time. Parts of the Battle of Ichi-no-Tani were fought in and around the grounds during the Genpei War, and markers in the Ikuta forest behind the shrine recall it.

The most recognisable photo is the red-lacquered tower gate (楼門) seen head-on from the street side. It fills the frame in strong vermilion, with the shrine's trees showing beyond it. Once you are inside, there are two quieter pictures. One is the tunnel of bright red torii gates at the Inari shrine, where a fox statue or two sits beside the path. The other is the Ikuta forest (生田の森), where tall trees and filtered light give a green, calmer backdrop.

Photography is not allowed inside the main hall. Try not to stand on the central path in front of the shrine. The torii row can be crowded at weekends, so be patient and shoot between groups of visitors.
text.geographic_location: Ikuta Shrine is in the Chūō Ward of Kobe, set in its own wooded grounds in the middle of the city. The tower gate faces the street and is the main entrance.
text.directions_text: Ikuta Shrine is in Chūō Ward, central Kobe. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Ikuta Shrine (生田神社). The tower gate is the main entrance on the street side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate seen head-on. If the gate is too big to fit from the street, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the torii tunnel, as it squeezes the gates closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the vermilion tower gate, facing the shrine from the street side). The red-lacquered tower gate filling the frame, with the shrine's grounds and trees visible beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the gate and turn on gridlines so the pillars stay straight. Leave a little room above the roof so the trees show behind it. For a different shot, the torii tunnel at the Inari shrine shows red gates receding into the distance with a fox statue at the side. The Ikuta forest paths are a greener, quieter alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red of the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the vermilion stays rich and does not wash out. For the torii tunnel, try a Live Photo, which may let you pick a frame with fewer people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day and on weekdays if you can, as the torii row can be crowded at weekends.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, and photography inside the main hall is not allowed, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any notices.
claims_not_in_sources: Going earlier in the day or on weekdays is likely to mean fewer people at the gates.
Slightly lowering the exposure helps keep strongly coloured red lacquer from washing out in bright light.
A telephoto lens makes a row of torii gates look closer together.

text.description: Kobe Meriken Park Oriental Hotel sits on the Harborland waterfront, close to Meriken Park. Its shape was designed by Takenaka Corporation to resemble a luxury liner, which gives the building a distinctive look beside the park. It has 14 floors and 331 rooms, so it is large enough to fill a frame with just a few steps of distance. The hotel opened in June 1995, only six months after the Great Hanshin earthquake destroyed much of the city, which gives the building a special place in Kobe's story. It is often pictured together with the Kobe Port Tower, so it makes a good pairing if you are collecting the classic Kobe harbour view. Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, because the strong horizontal lines of the building look best when straight. Tap on the hotel to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. If people are walking through the foreground, wait a moment for a clearer gap, or use them to add a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: In the Harborland waterfront area of Kobe, beside Meriken Park. The hotel is often photographed with the Kobe Port Tower nearby.
text.directions_text: Head for the Harborland and Meriken Park waterfront in Kobe. The hotel is 71 m to the south-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the hotel will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for details of the building's front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon up with a horizontal grid line. Keep the full hotel in the frame with some sky above it. If the Kobe Port Tower is in view, include it to the side as a second landmark. Step in a little for a tighter shot of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is washing out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk, when the sky is softer and the hotel's lights start to show. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The hotel is a working hotel and is best photographed from the outside; check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Kobe Mosque
label: Kobe Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '神戸モスク' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '神戸モスク' (node/13226873800): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Kobe Mosque'.
notes: Japan's oldest mosque, in the Kitano area.

text.description:
Kobe Mosque is Japan's first mosque, founded in October 1935, and it sits among the old Western-style houses of the Kitano-cho foreign district. That mix is part of the charm: a minaret and an onion-shaped dome in an Indo-Islamic style, in a district known for its old western-style buildings. It was designed by the Czech architect Jan Josef Švagr and built in reinforced concrete. It came through the 1945 air raids and the Great Hanshin earthquake of 1995, which is why some people call it the "Miracle Mosque".

It photographs well because the main frontage fits a lot into one picture. From the east side you can see the minaret with its balcony on the right, the dome on the left and the facade in the middle, all in a single shot. That gives you a clear, balanced photo without much fiddling.

The east side is the mosque's own car park, so treat it as a private space. Stay at the edge, keep clear of vehicles and doorways, and avoid taking photos while a prayer service is under way. This is a working place of worship, so don't photograph the inside unless you have been given permission. A short, polite visit with one or two good frames is plenty here.
text.geographic_location: Kobe Mosque is in the Kitano-cho foreign district of Chuo Ward, Kobe, at Nakayamate Dori. It is one of the best-known tourist areas of the city, full of old Western-style buildings.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from the Kitano-cho area and head for the mosque on Nakayamate Dori, looking for Kobe Mosque (神戸モスク). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which takes in the minaret, dome and facade together. If the car park is cramped and you can't step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), and keep the mosque away from the edges of the frame so it doesn't look stretched. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a closer shot of the dome or the minaret's balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (east side, from the mosque's eastern parking lot). The minaret with its balcony on the right of the frame and the onion-shaped dome on the left, with the mosque's facade in the middle. The mosque lies just to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the minaret on the right-hand line and the dome on the left, with the facade between them. Keep the phone level so the minaret stays upright. Stay at the car park's edge, out of the way of vehicles, and wait for people to walk out of shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the dome and minaret keep their detail. Take a couple of frames at slightly different zoom levels (1x and 2x) and choose the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the car park is quiet and no prayer service is on, and check for any posted service times on arrival or ask at the mosque.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, and the eastern car park is private, so ask permission before photographing the interior.

name: Kobe City Museum
label: Kobe City Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '京町筋' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '京町筋' (way/83468817): point nearest the subject (302 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/182530400: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kobe City Museum' (77 m across).

text.description: The Kobe City Museum is a neoclassical building from 1935, put up as the Kobe branch of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It became a museum in 1982, and the old bank's brick-and-stone frontage is the reason to bring your phone. The collection inside holds nearly thirty-nine thousand items, including archaeological finds, old maps, and Nanban art, plus Yayoi-period dōtaku from Sakuragaoka that are designated a National Treasure. From the street, though, it is the architecture you are photographing. The most effective picture is taken from street level, about 100 m north-east of the museum, with the phone held low and tilted slightly upwards. This makes the facade look taller and more imposing. A Kobe photography guide also recommends the building after dark, when it is lit up, so an evening visit can give you a very different picture from a daytime one. If you turn to look north up the street, the Hankyu Kobe-Sannomiya Building comes into the frame, which gives you a second, more urban composition. The building is on the west side of Kyomachisuji, so as a tip, cross to the opposite side of the street if you can to get the whole frontage in one shot. Keep your phone straight, with the gridlines on, so the columns and edges do not lean. Check the museum's current opening days before you go if you also want to see inside.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in central Kobe, on the west side of the street called Kyomachisuji. If you can, cross to the opposite side of Kyomachisuji from the frontage to fit the whole building in.
text.directions_text: The museum is in central Kobe, on Kyomachisuji. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole frontage in from across the street, then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the stonework and entrance details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 京町筋 (street opposite the museum's frontage, which sits on the west side of the street). The museum's historic brick-and-stone facade seen from street level, with a low angle that makes the building look more imposing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone low and tilt it slightly upwards so the building looks more imposing. Switch on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines. For a second picture, look north up the street, where the Hankyu Kobe-Sannomiya Building comes into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit stonework does not wash out in the evening. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against something steady or hold your breath as you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the building is illuminated. Daytime works too, but check lighting times before you go.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street; for opening days and entry to the museum itself, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens helps fit the whole frontage in when you are standing close across the street.
Crossing to the opposite side of Kyomachisuji from the frontage gives a view of the whole building.

text.description: Motomachi is a busy shopping district in Chūō Ward, Kobe, lying between Mount Rokkō and the port. It is best known for its mile-long covered shopping street. That makes it a good place for photos with depth: rows of shopfronts, signs and passers-by leading the eye down the arcade. The district has a cosmopolitan feel, and it is often compared with Motomachi in Yokohama, Ginza in Tokyo and Shinsaibashi in Osaka. In the 19th century many trading companies were based here. It sits right next to Nankinmachi (Kobe Chinatown) and the old foreign settlement of Kyū-kyoryūchi, where several buildings from that era now serve as restaurants or coffee shops. That gives you plenty of variety within a short walk: bright shopfronts, older façades, and street scenes with people in them. For the best phone shots, look for the long view down the arcade and keep the lines of the roof and shopfronts straight. Then move closer for details such as signs and window displays. Because the street is covered, the light is even, so you can often shoot without harsh shadows. Take a few wide shots to show the scale, then a few tighter ones that pick out one interesting shop or sign. Be considerate of people walking through, and avoid blocking the way while you frame your picture.
text.geographic_location: Motomachi is in Chūō Ward, central Kobe, between Mount Rokkō and the port. It sits next to Kobe's Chinatown (Nankinmachi) and the old foreign settlement area (Kyū-kyoryūchi).
text.directions_text: Motomachi Station (JR Kobe Line, Hanshin Main Line and Kobe Rapid Transit Tōzai Line) serves the district. Once you get there, look for the covered shopping street nearby. That makes it a good photo stop for visitors who want a picture that says 'this is a port city'. You can include open sky and the building in one frame, which suits a phone well.

One small fact helps with expectations: the Yamato 1 and the TSL Hayate, two former exhibits, were removed in 2016, so you won't see them any more. Treat the museum building as the subject.

Then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit everything in, and keep the phone level so the building's lines stay upright. Gridlines in the camera settings help with this. If other visitors are passing, wait a moment for a gap. Finish with a tighter shot on the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out roof shapes or details.

The spot is quick to visit.

text.description:
The Kobe Anpanman Children's Museum & Mall is an interactive museum built around Takashi Yanase's Anpanman characters, which are hugely popular with children in Japan. It is one of five such complexes in the country, the others being in Yokohama, Sendai, Nagoya and Fukuoka. Kobe's opened in 2013, which makes it the newest of the five. The complex is fairly big, roughly 94 metres across.

The museum is dedicated to Anpanman, which gives you a fun subject for a photo even if you never go in. For a phone photo, the easiest approach is to take one clear shot of the whole frontage from a little way back, then move closer for one or two details, using any interesting details you can see. If people are in the scene, wait a moment for a gap or include them as part of the picture. If you do photograph strangers' children, keep them small in the frame or turn them away from the camera. Take a quick look at the result and retake it if the sky has washed out. If you plan to go inside, check the official site first for entry details and any rules about taking photos indoors.

name: Sōraku-en
label: Sorakuen Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sōraku-en' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/180597618: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sorakuen Garden' (265 m across).
notes: Japanese garden with a historic house.

text.description: Sōraku-en is one of the few historic Japanese gardens inside Kobe, and it is a calm place to take photographs in the middle of the city. It is a stroll garden, so a path leads you round a central pond, and the view changes with every few steps. The garden was once part of the home of Kodera Yasujirō and has belonged to the city since 1941. Most of the old house was lost in the war, but the stable of 1907 survived and is now an Important Cultural Property. That stable is the best subject here. Stand at the pond edge, face the stable and let the still water show its reflection, with the garden greenery all around. Elsewhere in the grounds you can also find the former Hassam Residence, an Edo-period boathouse-style building, a teahouse and a very large camphor tree that was growing here before the house was built. The garden became a Place of Scenic Beauty in 2006. The historic buildings can only be photographed from the outside, so plan your pictures from the paths and the water's edge. If you have time, walk on to the teahouse on the far bank of the pond, or to the stone bridge, where stream and rockwork fill the frame. Both make good second shots.
text.geographic_location: Sōraku-en is in Chūō Ward, Kobe, at Nakayamatedōri, in the Motomachi area close to the city centre.
text.directions_text: Start from Motomachi or Kenchō-mae station, which are both close to the garden. Head for Nakayamatedōri in Chūō Ward and follow your map app to the garden entrance. Once inside, walk to the pond and you will reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the stable and its reflection. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the pond, trees and buildings in one frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the teahouse across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you face the former Kodera Stable, and its reflection shows in the water with the garden greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the stable on one third, with the reflection filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the water looks flat and the buildings stand straight. For a second picture, frame the teahouse on the far bank between the water and the trees, or include the stone bridge and rockwork. The historic buildings can only be photographed from outside, so keep to the paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water just beside the stable to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and bright leaves keep their colour. Wait for any ripples to settle before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning light suits the reflection. The garden is also popular in November during the autumn illumination period, so expect more people then and check the dates before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed public garden with a small entry fee, so check the official site before you go for opening times, fees and any special evening openings.

name: Kobe Luminarie
label: Kobe Luminarie
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '神戸市役所1号館' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '神戸市役所1号館' (way/182530152): middle (68 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1636567: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Winter light festival at the old foreign settlement.

text.description:
Kobe Luminarie is a festival of lights that began in 1995 as a tribute to the people of Kobe after the Great Hanshin earthquake of that year. The lights were a gift from the Italian Government, and more than 200,000 hand-painted bulbs are lit in elaborate arches and walls. The display usually stays up for about two weeks and is switched on for only a few hours each evening. Since the festival returned in January 2024, the displays have been spread across several sites in Kobe, so check the official site for this year's layout, dates and any paid areas.

The best overview is from the 24th-floor observation lobby of Kobe City Hall No. 1 Building (神戸市役所1号館). From up there you look down on the light route and Higashi Yuenchi Park together, and you can see how the installation is laid out, which you can't judge from street level. Visitor guides describe the lobby as free to enter, but its opening hours haven't been confirmed, so check before you go.

For a second picture, go down to Higashi Yuenchi Park and shoot the roughly 50-metre illuminated wall head-on from the open ground in front of it. The arched corridor along Nakamachi-dori also works well with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x). Tripods are prohibited, so plan to shoot handheld.
text.geographic_location: Central Kobe, around Higashi Yuenchi Park and the old Foreign Settlement area, with Kobe City Hall No. 1 Building looking down on the route. The exact festival layout changes from year to year.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use the official site or a map app to find your way to Kobe City Hall No. 1 Building. Follow the crowds and the festival signs once you are at street level. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole route and park from above. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the crowd below, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) for the street-level arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 神戸市役所1号館 (24th-floor observation lobby). A high, elevated overview of the whole light route and Higashi Yuenchi Park below, looking down on the installations.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the lines to keep the route running diagonally through the frame, with the park crowd at the bottom for scale. If you go down to the park, shoot the roughly 50-metre illuminated wall straight on from the open ground in front of it. Along Nakamachi-dori, use the ultra-wide lens to fit in the full arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest lights to focus, then lower the exposure slider so the bulbs keep their colour instead of washing out to white. Use night mode if your phone offers it and keep your elbows tight against your body or a ledge to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the lights are on. They are lit only for a few hours each evening, so arrive early. The next edition is listed as roughly late January to early February 2027, but confirm dates and hours on the official site.

text.access_note: The festival has its own dates and some areas may be ticketed or restricted, and the City Hall lobby's hours have not been confirmed, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Kitano-chō, also known as Kitano Ijinkan, is a historic district of Kobe where a number of foreign residences from the late Meiji and early Taishō eras still stand. The word ijinkan can describe any foreign house of that period in Japan, but it is most often used for the ones here, because so many have survived. Hakodate and Nagasaki have similar districts, though these are not as well preserved. Some of the houses are still lived in, and many are open to visitors, which makes this one of the main places for tourists in Kobe.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the mix of old Western-style architecture and everyday streets. You can shoot a whole house from across the lane, then step closer for details such as windows, doorways, balconies and roof lines. Turn on the gridlines so the walls and rooflines stay straight, and take a few frames of each house from slightly different distances.

Walk south from there and take photos as you go rather than waiting for one perfect view. Many houses are open to visitors. Please keep to the public lanes and respect the homes that are still private residences.
text.geographic_location: Kitano-chō is a historic district of Kobe, in Hyōgo Prefecture, known for its cluster of former foreign residences.
